Solutions 1 and 3 give the same exponent, since (q−2)/(k/2−1) = 2(q−2)/(k−2). Solution 2 gives a different one. I did not derive the exponent from scratch. I am relying on a plausibility check and a vague recollection of the literature on this problem.

**Check on Solution 2.** Its exponent (k−2)/(k−q+1) equals 1 at q = 3, so the weakest condition would already need nearly n colors. At q = k/2+1 it exceeds 1, giving (k−2)/(k/2), which is just under 2. The dimension coloring with n colors already gives every C_k at least k/2 colors, and that is far below q = k/2+1 only by one, so an exponent above 1 at the top of the range looks implausible. Its justification is also a bare assertion with no real argument.

**Check on Solutions 1 and 3.** The exponent (q−2)/(k/2−1) grows with q. It is 1/(k/2−1) at q = 3 and reaches 1 at q = k/2+1. This is the behaviour one expects, and it matches my vague recollection of the known result. The supporting arguments in both solutions are heuristic. Solution 3 also has some sloppy table entries, such as calling α = 1 "sublinear" and miscomputing the k = 6, q = 3 case. Its final answer is nonetheless the same as Solution 1's.

I pick Solution 1.

CHOICE: 1
